name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_THELIVINGWORLD_MCQ_Q01 - Number of common characteristics from species to kingdom

questiontext.text: As we go from species to kingdom in a taxonomic hierarchy, the number of common characteristics

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In a taxonomic hierarchy, organisms are grouped into progressively broader categories moving from species up to kingdom: Species \(\rightarrow\) Genus \(\rightarrow\) Family \(\rightarrow\) Order \(\rightarrow\) Class \(\rightarrow\) Phylum (or Division) \(\rightarrow\) Kingdom.

Step 2: Evaluation
A species consists of closely related individuals sharing the maximum number of common characteristics. As we ascend the hierarchy toward the kingdom, more diverse groups of organisms are included in each successive category.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Because the inclusivity of organisms increases at higher taxonomic levels, the number of shared or common characteristics among them decreases. Therefore, as we go from species to kingdom, the number of common characteristics will decrease.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_THELIVINGWORLD_MCQ_Q02 - Suffix indicating plant taxonomic category of family

questiontext.text: Which of the following 'suffixes' used for units of classification in plants indicates a taxonomic category of 'family'?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Under the International Code of Botanical Nomenclature (ICBN), standardized suffixes are assigned to different taxonomic ranks in plant classification to make their hierarchical level immediately recognizable.

Step 2: Evaluation
In botanical nomenclature, the suffix "-aceae" denotes a family (for example, Solanaceae, Fabaceae, Liliaceae). In contrast, "-ales" denotes an order (for example, Polymoniales), while "-onae" and "-ae" are not the standard suffixes for a plant family.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The suffix used for units of classification in plants that indicates the taxonomic category of family is "– Aceae".

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_THELIVINGWORLD_MCQ_Q03 - Definition and scope of the term systematics

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Systematics is derived from the Latin word systema, meaning systematic arrangement of organisms. It encompasses the study of the diversity of organisms and their comparative and evolutionary relationships.

Step 2: Evaluation
Systematics goes beyond mere identification, preservation, or study of organ systems and habitats. It integrates taxonomy (characterization, identification, classification, and nomenclature) with evolutionary relationships among different kinds of organisms.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the term systematics refers to the diversity of kinds of organisms and their relationship.

answer.text: Identification and study of organ systems of plants and animals
Identification and preservation of plants and animals
Diversity of kinds of organisms and their relationship
Study of habitats of organisms and their classification

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_THELIVINGWORLD_MCQ_Q04 - Meaning of the taxonomic category genus

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In the taxonomic hierarchy, a genus is the taxonomic rank immediately above species and below family.

Step 2: Evaluation
A genus comprises a group of closely related species that have more characters in common compared to species of other genera. For example, potato (Solanum tuberosum) and brinjal (Solanum melongena) are two different species belonging to the same genus Solanum. A genus does not represent a single individual or an arbitrary collection of unrelated organisms.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, genus represents a group of closely related species of plants or animals.

answer.text: A group of closely related species of plants or animals

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_THELIVINGWORLD_MCQ_Q05 - Plant taxonomic level equivalent to animal phylum

questiontext.text: The taxonomic unit 'Phylum' in the classification of animals is equivalent to which hierarchical level in classification of plants

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In biological classification, the hierarchical sequence from species to kingdom is Species \(\rightarrow\) Genus \(\rightarrow\) Family \(\rightarrow\) Order \(\rightarrow\) Class \(\rightarrow\) Phylum/Division \(\rightarrow\) Kingdom.

Step 2: Evaluation
In animal taxonomy, the category comprising classes with a few similar characters just below the kingdom level is called Phylum. In plant taxonomy, the exact equivalent hierarchical rank below Kingdom and above Class is called Division.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the taxonomic unit Phylum in animals is equivalent to Division in the classification of plants.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_THELIVINGWORLD_MCQ_Q06 - Types of species in botanical gardens and zoological parks

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Botanical gardens and zoological parks are specialized ex-situ taxonomical aids that maintain collections of living plants and wild animals, respectively, for identification, research, education, and conservation.

Step 2: Evaluation
These facilities are not restricted to only local, only endemic, or only exotic species. Instead, they house both endemic (native to a specific region) and exotic (introduced from other regions) living species under protected and simulated natural conditions.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, botanical gardens and zoological parks have a collection of endemic and exotic living species.

answer.text: Collection of endemic and exotic living species
Collection of only local plants and animals

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_THELIVINGWORLD_MCQ_Q07 - Use of taxonomic key in monographs and flora

questiontext.text: Taxonomic key is one of the taxonomic tools in the identification and classification of plants and animals. It is used in the preparation of

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A taxonomic key is an analytical tool used for the identification of plants and animals based on contrasting characters arranged in pairs called couplets.

Step 2: Evaluation
Taxonomic keys are used in preparing both monographs (which contain comprehensive information on any one taxon) and flora (which provide the actual account of habitat and distribution of plants of a given area and help in their identification).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, a taxonomic key is used in the preparation of both monographs and flora.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_THELIVINGWORLD_MCQ_Q08 - Reason all living organisms are linked to one another

questiontext.text: All living organisms are linked to one another because

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
All living organisms—present, past, and future—are linked to one another by the sharing of common genetic material, though to varying degrees of similarity.

Step 2: Evaluation
While organisms share genetic material (DNA or RNA), it is not identical ("of the same type") across all species; rather, the degree of similarity varies according to evolutionary relatedness. Furthermore, cellular organization is not identical across all organisms (for example, prokaryotes lack membrane-bound organelles, whereas eukaryotes possess them).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, all living organisms are linked to one another because they share common genetic material but to varying degrees.

answer.text: They have common genetic material of the same type
They share common genetic material but to varying degrees

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_THELIVINGWORLD_MCQ_Q09 - Defining characteristic of living organisms

questiontext.text: Which of the following is a defining characteristic of living organisms?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A defining characteristic of living organisms must be present in all living organisms without exception and must not be exhibited by non-living objects.

Step 2: Evaluation
Growth (an increase in mass and size) is not a defining property because non-living things like mountains, boulders, and sand mounds also grow by external accumulation of material. Reproduction is also not an all-inclusive defining feature because several living organisms, such as mules, sterile worker bees, and infertile human couples, cannot reproduce. Making sound is not universal across living organisms (such as plants and microbes). However, consciousness—the ability to sense the environment and respond to external stimuli—is exhibited by all living organisms from prokaryotes to complex eukaryotes.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, response to external stimuli is a defining characteristic of living organisms.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_THELIVINGWORLD_MCQ_Q10 - Matching taxonomic categories of potato plant

questiontext.text: Match the following and choose the correct option:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Each taxonomic category in the classification of a plant, such as potato (Solanum tuberosum), is identified by standard nomenclature rules and suffixes.

Step 2: Evaluation

  • Family: Plant family names end with the suffix "-aceae"; thus, Family matches Solanacea (Solanaceae).
  • Kingdom: All plants belong to the Kingdom Plantae.
  • Order: Plant order names end with the suffix "-ales"; thus, Order matches Polymoniales.
  • Species: In binomial nomenclature, the second word is the specific epithet; for potato, Species matches tuberosum.
  • Genus: The first word of the binomial name represents the genus; thus, Genus matches Solanum.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairs are: Family – Solanacea, Kingdom – Plantae, Order – Polymoniales, Species – tuberosum, and Genus – Solanum.
